strengths: The paper addresses a relevant combination of problems in continual semantic segmentation: forgetting, class imbalance, and separation of future classes within the background. Transferring a learned cluster-assignment model across tasks is a potentially useful contribution. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-01/reviews/b03/review-experiment-hyk42ht2/call-603e3a9a6ae64f369373529ee19d8276/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The empirical evaluation is substantial, covering ADE20K, Pascal VOC, and Cityscapes, several incremental schedules, and convolutional and Transformer segmentation models. In Table 6, Transformer-based FALCON achieves 41.9/40.3 mIoU on ADE20K 100-50/100-10, compared with FairCL's 37.6/35.5. Its contribution does not depend on outperforming every competing method in every setting.

The ablations provide meaningful evidence of practical benefits. In Table 1, the fairness loss increases minority-class mIoU from 26.4 to 30.8 on ADE20K 100-50 while also improving majority-class performance. Table 2 supports adapting the visual grammar across tasks, and Table 5 reports only a 0.5-point decline on initial classes over six steps. The supplementary sensitivity studies and implementation settings are useful.
weaknesses: The central theoretical interpretation is not established. Propositions 1–2 characterize optimal normalized softmax probabilities, but their dependence on class size does not establish cluster compactness or fairness. Duplicating identical features decreases their individual probabilities without changing compactness. Consequently, the inference in Section 3.2 that smaller enforcement values imply tighter clusters is unjustified. Appendix 9 also invokes a triangle inequality without establishing that the proposed contrastive loss is a metric; discarding an additive constant through Big-O notation does not establish the claimed distillation guarantee.

The stated optimization leaves a consequential ambiguity. Equation (8) minimizes over network parameters, whereas the cluster regularizer depends only on centroids described as frozen or momentum-updated; Appendix 9 explicitly treats them as constants during loss computation. Under that description, the regularizer has no gradient to the segmentation network. The manuscript does not specify an alternative gradient path that explains its measured improvements in Table 4. This affects the reproducibility of a claimed component, rather than merely its presentation.

The experiments do not fully isolate the proposed mechanisms. Section 4.2 states that removing visual grammar also reduces the unknown clusters to one, coupling assignment strategy with background representation capacity. A comparison using identical multiple-cluster initialization would better identify the attention model's contribution. Likewise, comparisons with existing balanced contrastive losses or straightforward class reweighting are absent, leaving the advantage of the particular fairness formulation insufficiently distinguished from related approaches.

Important implementation details remain unspecified despite the appendix, including DBSCAN neighborhood and minimum-sample settings, selection of unknown pixels from background containing old classes, and the visual-grammar pretraining schedule. Computational overhead is also unreported despite the additional 12-layer attention model, clustering, and repeated feature extraction.

Overall, the consistent benchmark gains and demonstrated minority-class improvements make this a credible empirical contribution. However, the unsupported theoretical conclusions and unresolved optimization specification prevent a confident acceptance recommendation. These substantive concerns, balanced against the experimental strengths, place the manuscript near the decision boundary.
